tips.title: Orange to colourless, never clear
tips.body: Bromine water is **orange**; an **alkene** decolourises it. Write **colourless**, because orange bromine water is already clear in the see-through sense, and clear is not a colour. An **alkane** gives **no change**.

tips.title: Two fewer hydrogens means an alkene
tips.body: Work out what the **alkane** with that many carbons would be, using $2n+2$. If the formula has **two fewer** hydrogens, it is an **alkene**. C₈H₁₆ against C₈H₁₈ settles it without knowing any names.

tips.title: Subtract to find the missing product
tips.body: For a cracking equation, subtract the carbons and subtract the hydrogens. Whatever is left accounts for the **rest of the products**. C₁₀H₂₂ minus C₈H₁₈ leaves 2 carbons and 4 hydrogens, so C₂H₄. Check whether the remainder is one molecule or **two** of a smaller alkene.

tips.title: Cracking has two justifications
tips.body: A question on why cracking matters wants **both**: the **fuels** argument, since demand for small molecules is high, and the **feedstock** argument, since alkenes make **polymers and many other chemicals**. Giving only the fuels half caps the marks.

why.matters:
Fractional distillation gives you whatever the barrel happened to contain, and that is not what anybody wants to buy. There is far too much heavy, sluggish, long-chain oil and never enough petrol.

**Cracking** fixes the mismatch by breaking long molecules into short ones — and it does something better than that as a side effect. The pieces cannot all be alkanes, so one of them comes out with a double bond, and that alkene is the raw material for almost every plastic there is.

examples.title: Turning what nobody wants into what everybody does
examples.body:
A refinery can sell every litre of petrol it can make and is left with heavy fractions it can barely give away. Cracking converts one into the other: heat the long molecules until they break, either over a **hot catalyst** or mixed with **steam**.

Nothing is added. A long chain becomes a shorter chain plus something else, and the shorter chain is petrol. That is why a refinery is not just a separation plant: the column decides what crude oil gives you, and cracking decides what you sell.

visual.alt: A flow chart of cracking: a long-chain fraction is heated to a vapour and passed over a hot catalyst or mixed with steam, giving a shorter alkane that can be sold as petrol and an alkene alongside it

examples.title: The half of the reaction that becomes a plastic
examples.body:
Break a four-carbon molecule in two and the pieces cannot both be alkanes: there are not enough hydrogens to go round. One piece takes a **double bond** instead and comes out as an alkene.

That shortfall is the most useful accident in the oil industry. Ethene is what poly(ethene) is made from, and the same double bond is what lets alkenes be turned into alcohols and everything built on them. The petrol pays for the cracker; the alkene is why it is worth running.

props.title: The atoms have to balance either side

visual.alt: The cracking of butane drawn as structures: a four-carbon chain breaking into a two-carbon ethane and a two-carbon ethene with a double bond, the hydrogens balancing at ten on each side

examples.title: The orange water that goes clear
examples.body:
Two colourless liquids, both hydrocarbons, and one test tells them apart in a second. Shake each with **bromine water**: the alkane leaves it orange, and the alkene turns it colourless.

The double bond is the reason. It can **open up** and take the bromine across it, which uses the bromine up and takes the colour with it. An alkane has no double bond and nothing to offer, so the bromine stays as it was. The test is not a colour change so much as a reaction happening or not happening.

visual.alt: A table setting an alkane against an alkene: the alkane has no carbon to carbon double bond and leaves bromine water orange, while the alkene has one and turns the bromine water colourless

steps.title: Why crack anything at all
steps.body:
Fractional distillation gives you whatever crude oil happens to contain, and that is not what the world wants to buy.

Crude oil yields a great deal of **long-chain** hydrocarbon, which is thick, hard to ignite and of limited use. Meanwhile there is a **high demand for fuels with small molecules**, such as petrol, because those are the ones that vaporise and burn readily.

**Cracking** solves the mismatch. Long hydrocarbon molecules are **broken down into smaller, more useful molecules**.

The products are of two kinds, and this is the key fact of the topic.

- Some are **alkanes**, which go straight into fuels.
- Some are a different type of hydrocarbon called **alkenes**.

Alkenes matter because they are the **starting materials for polymers and for many other chemicals**. So cracking does two useful jobs at once: it converts surplus long molecules into fuels people want, and it produces the alkenes the chemical industry needs.

steps.title: The two methods
steps.body:
You should be able to describe **in general terms** the conditions used for the two methods named in the specification.

- **Catalytic cracking**: the vapour is passed over a **hot catalyst**.
- **Steam cracking**: the vapour is mixed with **steam** and heated to a **very high temperature**.

Both start the same way: the fraction is **heated until it vaporises**. What differs is what happens to the vapour next.

The specification says *in general terms*, which is a useful hint. You are not expected to quote exact temperatures or name the catalyst. "A hot catalyst" and "steam and a very high temperature" are what the mark scheme is looking for, and adding an invented number can only lose you credit.

steps.title: Alkanes and alkenes side by side
steps.body:
Cracking produces alkanes and **alkenes**, so you need to tell them apart.

The simplest test on paper is to **count the hydrogens** for the number of carbons you have.

- An **alkane** follows $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+2}$.
- An **alkene** has **two fewer hydrogens** for the same number of carbons.

So for two carbons, C₂H₆ is the alkane and C₂H₄ is the alkene. For three, C₃H₈ against C₃H₆.

The chemical difference that matters here is **reactivity**: **alkenes are more reactive than alkanes**. That single fact drives both the test for them and their use in making polymers.

Alkenes react with **bromine water**, and that reaction is **used as a test for alkenes**.

steps.title: The bromine water test
steps.body:
This is the one colour change in the topic, and it must be stated precisely.

**Bromine water is orange. An alkene turns it colourless.**

- Add bromine water to an **alkene**: the orange colour **disappears**, leaving a **colourless** solution.
- Add it to an **alkane**: **no change**, the bromine water stays orange.

Two words cost marks here.

- Write **colourless**, not "clear". Orange bromine water is already clear, in the sense of being see-through. Clear is not a colour.
- Bromine water is usually described as **orange**, and orange to colourless is the answer. If a question calls it brown, follow the question's own wording, but never say it turns white or transparent.

So the test is: add bromine water and shake. Decolourised means an alkene is present.

steps.title: Balancing a cracking equation
steps.body:
You are expected to **balance cracking equations given the formulae**. The rule is simple, and it is the only check you need:

**every carbon and every hydrogen that goes in must come out**.

Cracking splits one large molecule into smaller ones, so whatever is missing from the fragment you are given must account for the rest. Usually that is a single second product, but check: a remainder of C₄H₈ could equally be **two** molecules of C₂H₄, and AQA equations often have two alkene molecules on the right.

steps.text: So the other product has $10 - 8 = 2$ carbons
So the other product has $22 - 18 = 4$ hydrogens
Two carbons and four hydrogens is C₂H₄, an **alkene**

check.prompt: C₈H₁₈ is cracked to give C₆H₁₄ and one other product. What is the other product?
check.solution: Carbon: $8 - 6 = 2$. Hydrogen: $18 - 14 = 4$. So the other product is **C₂H₄**, an alkene. $$C₈H₁₈ → C₆H₁₄ + C₂H₄$$

steps.title: Your turn: working both ways
steps.body:
1. C₁₂H₂₆ is cracked. One product is C₄H₁₀. Work out the formula of the other product, and say whether it is an alkane or an alkene.
2. Write the balanced equation.
3. Describe how you could show experimentally that the second product is an alkene, including what you would see.
4. Give **two** reasons why an oil company would want to crack C₁₂H₂₆ at all.

For part 4, one reason is about fuels and the other is about the chemical industry. A full answer needs both.

visuals.alt: A blank table for working out the second product of a cracking reaction by counting atoms

check.prompt: C₁₂H₂₆ is cracked to give C₄H₁₀ and one other product. What is it?
check.solution: Carbon: $12 - 4 = 8$. Hydrogen: $26 - 10 = 16$. Eight carbons with sixteen hydrogens is **C₈H₁₆**, an alkene, since an alkane with eight carbons would need eighteen. $$C₁₂H₂₆ → C₄H₁₀ + C₈H₁₆$$

steps.title: Going deeper: why cracking is worth doing
steps.body:
A question asking you to **explain the usefulness of cracking**, or **how modern life depends on hydrocarbons**, is worth several marks and is often answered with one.

There are **two separate justifications**, and a full answer gives both.

**First, the fuels argument.** Crude oil supplies more long-chain hydrocarbon than anyone wants, and less short-chain than everyone needs. Cracking converts the surplus into the shortage: there is a **high demand for fuels with small molecules**, and **some of the products of cracking are useful as fuels**. A refinery can therefore match what it produces to what the market wants, rather than being stuck with whatever the oil contained.

**Second, the feedstock argument.** Cracking produces **alkenes**, and alkenes are **used to produce polymers** and are the **starting materials for the production of many other chemicals**. Without cracking there would be very little supply of alkenes, and therefore very little of the plastics industry.

That second point is what the phrase *modern life depends on hydrocarbons* is pointing at. Fuels are the obvious half. The less obvious half is that the same barrel of oil provides the raw material for plastics, and both halves run through cracking.

One honest complication worth having ready if a question invites evaluation: everything above is an argument about **usefulness**, not about whether it is problem-free. Crude oil remains **finite**, and burning its products releases carbon dioxide. Cracking makes better use of a finite resource; it does not make it renewable.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Cracking** breaks large hydrocarbon molecules down into **smaller, more useful** molecules.
- Methods include **catalytic cracking**, passing the vapour over a **hot catalyst**, and **steam cracking**, mixing it with **steam at a very high temperature**.
- Describe the conditions **in general terms**. Exact temperatures and catalyst names are not required.
- The products include **alkanes** and another type of hydrocarbon called **alkenes**.
- An alkene has **two fewer hydrogens** than the alkane with the same number of carbons: C₂H₆ against C₂H₄.
- **Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes.**
- Alkenes **react with bromine water**, which is **used as the test for alkenes**.
- The colour change is **orange to colourless**. Say colourless, never clear. An alkane gives **no change**.
- To balance a cracking equation, make sure **every carbon and hydrogen in comes out**: C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₂H₄.
- There is a **high demand for fuels with small molecules**, so some products of cracking are useful as **fuels**.
- Alkenes are used to produce **polymers** and are **starting materials for many other chemicals**.
- Cracking makes better use of a **finite** resource. It does not make crude oil renewable.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Finding the product.** Carbon: $10 - 8 = 2$. Hydrogen: $22 - 18 = 4$. So the other product is **C₂H₄**.

$$C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₂H₄$$

Both carbon and hydrogen balance: $10 = 8 + 2$ and $22 = 18 + 4$.

**The test.** Add **bromine water** to each product and shake. The **alkene** turns it from **orange to colourless**, because alkenes are **more reactive** than alkanes. The **alkane** gives **no change**: the bromine water stays orange.

Write **colourless**, not clear. Orange bromine water is already see-through.

questions.prompt: Explain why oil companies crack long-chain hydrocarbons, giving two separate reasons, and explain why cracking does not solve the problem that crude oil is finite.
questions.solution: The first reason concerns fuels. Crude oil contains far more long-chain hydrocarbon than anyone wants to buy, because long-chain molecules are viscous and hard to ignite, while there is a high demand for fuels with small molecules such as petrol, which vaporise and burn readily. Cracking breaks the surplus long molecules down into smaller, more useful ones, and some of the products of cracking are useful as fuels, so a refinery can match what it produces to what the market actually wants. The second reason concerns the chemical industry. Cracking also produces alkenes, which are a different type of hydrocarbon, and alkenes are used to produce polymers and are the starting materials for the production of many other chemicals. Without cracking there would be very little supply of alkenes and therefore very little of the plastics industry. However, cracking does not address the fact that crude oil is finite. It creates no new crude oil, it simply rearranges the molecules that were already in the barrel, so it makes better use of a limited resource rather than making that resource renewable, and the oil will still eventually run out.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Reason 1: fuels.** Crude oil contains **more long-chain hydrocarbon than anyone wants** — it is viscous and hard to ignite — while there is a **high demand for fuels with small molecules** such as petrol, which vaporise and burn readily. Cracking breaks the surplus down into **smaller, more useful** molecules, and **some of the products are useful as fuels**, so a refinery can match its output to demand.

**Reason 2: feedstock.** Cracking also produces **alkenes**, which are **used to produce polymers** and are **starting materials for many other chemicals**. Without cracking there would be little supply of alkenes, and little of the plastics industry.

**Why it does not solve the finite problem.** Cracking creates **no new crude oil**. It rearranges molecules that were already in the barrel, so it makes **better use** of a limited resource rather than making it renewable. The oil will still run out.

examTechnique.body:
For a cracking equation, count carbon and then hydrogen, and **subtract**. The fragment that is left is the other product, and the subtraction is also your check.

To decide whether a product is an alkene, work out what the **alkane** with that many carbons would be. Two fewer hydrogens means an alkene.

For the test, name **bromine water**, and give **both** results: orange to **colourless** for the alkene, **no change** for the alkane. A test question with only the positive result is half an answer.

Write **colourless**. Clear is not a colour and does not earn the mark.

For the conditions, stay in general terms: **a hot catalyst**, or **steam at a very high temperature**. Inventing a figure risks contradicting the mark scheme.

For usefulness, give **two** arguments: fuels, because demand for small molecules is high, and alkenes, because they make polymers and other chemicals.
examinerErrors: Writing that bromine water turns clear rather than colourless.
Giving only the positive result of the test and not saying what an alkane does.
Confusing cracking with fractional distillation. Distillation separates; cracking breaks molecules up.
Saying alkanes are more reactive than alkenes. It is the other way round.
Leaving a cracking equation unbalanced, usually by losing hydrogens.
Quoting an exact temperature or catalyst name that the specification does not require.
Giving only the fuels reason for cracking, and omitting alkenes as a feedstock.
Claiming cracking makes crude oil renewable. It remains finite.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer finds the missing product by subtraction rather than recognition, and shows the carbon and hydrogen counts on both sides as its own check. It identifies an alkene by comparing with the alkane formula for the same number of carbons, so it never needs a name it has not been taught. In the test it gives both outcomes and uses the word colourless deliberately. Asked why cracking matters, it separates the fuels argument from the feedstock argument and states both, and if the question invites evaluation it adds that cracking makes better use of a finite resource without making it renewable.
